S1_incident_reporting.quote: Manufacturers must report every thermal incident involving overheating, fire, injury, or material property damage to the relevant regulator within 24 hours of becoming aware of it, and provide a complete incident report within 10 business days. They must notify affected customers within 72 hours when an incident indicates a material safety risk or requires inspection, mitigation, or product action.

S2_thermal_testing.quote: Each model must undergo a sustained-heat test at 55 °C. The failure rate must not exceed 5% for any model, except where the regulator grants a time-limited, model-specific variance after reviewing independent test results and a documented corrective-action plan. A variance must specify interim safeguards, customer notices, milestones, and a short expiration date; it may be renewed only after review of progress and updated evidence. Manufacturers must provide the per-model test results, including the failure rate, to customers considering or purchasing that model; results may not be withheld from those customers as confidential. Individual-company per-model failure rates need not be published to the general public.

S3_remote_shutoff.quote: All new home battery models placed on the market 12 months or more after adoption must support remote emergency shut-off. For installed units, manufacturers must provide a remote-shutoff retrofit or equivalent compliant upgrade within 6 years after adoption, where technically feasible; any units not upgraded must be identified to their customers and the regulator with interim risk-mitigation instructions.

S4_fire_suppression.quote: All new home battery units manufactured 36 months or more after adoption must include built-in fire suppression meeting the applicable performance requirements. Manufacturers must provide customers and regulators with evidence of compliance.

S5_customer_disclosure.quote: Customers must receive clear safety notices promptly when a known incident or test result indicates a material risk or requires inspection, mitigation, or product action. A recall is mandatory when a model exceeds 8 thermal incidents per 100,000 installed units in any 12-month period. Manufacturers must promptly notify the regulator and affected customers, stop distribution of the affected model pending regulatory direction, and carry out the regulator-approved recall or corrective action.

document.section_notes: S1 is strict and uniform (all incidents reported within 24 hours, customer notice within 72 hours, no phase-in) and hurts both firms' reporting gaps equally. S2 keeps the 55 °C / 5% standard and gives purchasers numeric results while avoiding public publication, but the open-ended, renewable regulator variance can keep an over-limit model (e.g., the Hearth 10 at 6.2%) on sale indefinitely, which is a Northwind win and a weakening. S3 and S4 sit inside their acceptable ranges (12-month new-unit shut-off, 6-year retrofit with an alternative-notice escape, 36-month built-in suppression), while S5 pairs the safe 8/100,000 mandatory recall trigger with an unbounded regulator-approved corrective-action alternative and only 'prompt' notices, a Halcyon win that weakens the section.
